opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the short answer is that we don't have a great way to assess it yet, and that's part of what motivated some of our work.

One experiment we did, together with Kaiming He, revisits an old idea from Torralba and Efros about a decade ago called "Name That Dataset." Back then, datasets were small and fairly curated, and it turned out you could train a classifier to tell which dataset an image came from. That was a sign that each dataset had its own bias, its own "signature." The hope over the following years was that as we moved to these huge, internet-scale collections like YFCC, Conceptual Captions, LAION, and DataComp, that bias would wash out. If you scrape billions of images from the web, surely you're just sampling "the visual world," right?

So we tried the same thing with modern datasets and modern networks. We took a few of these large web-scale datasets, which on the surface look very similar, all natural images of everyday stuff, and trained a standard ConvNet or ViT to predict which dataset each image came from. Surprisingly, the models do this very well, far above chance, even on held-out images. As humans we really struggle with that task; if you look at the images yourself, it's hard to say what distinguishes them. But the networks pick up on something, whether it's the collection pipeline, the filtering, the captioning source, or subtle distributional differences in content and style. And it's not just memorization. The features they learn for this task transfer reasonably well to other tasks, so they're capturing something semantic about how these datasets differ.

To me, the takeaway is that "internet-scale" doesn't mean "unbiased" or "covers everything." Each of these datasets is still a particular slice of the visual world, shaped by decisions people made when building it. If two giant datasets that are supposed to represent the same thing are this easy to tell apart, then neither of them is really the whole distribution.

So when people ask whether a dataset is broad enough to generalize to every task, I'd frame it differently. Rather than relying only on downstream benchmarks, which tend to share many of the same biases as the training data, we need diagnostics that probe the data itself. Dataset classification is one crude but useful probe: if you can easily separate your dataset from others, that tells you there's structure your model might be overfitting to. Beyond that, you want to look at coverage of rare concepts, long-tail domains like medical, scientific, or industrial imagery, different geographies and cultures, and nonstandard viewpoints. Those are exactly where web data is thin.

My honest view is that current web-scale datasets are remarkably good for a lot of tasks, much better than anything we had before, but they're not "everything." The gap shows up in the tails, and we should be measuring that directly instead of assuming scale alone will solve it.

r001.rationale: It describes training a ConvNet or ViT to predict which large web-scale dataset each image came from.

r002.rationale: It says the models distinguish seemingly similar large datasets well, even on held-out images.

r003.rationale: It says no individual dataset captures the whole visual world, but does not question whether an all-encompassing distribution is a well-defined dataset target.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that we don't have a good way to assess it, and the ways we currently try are a bit circular.

The standard move is to take a dataset, train a model on it, and then measure transfer on a suite of downstream benchmarks. And on that measure, things look great. You pretrain on LAION or on some internal web-scale dataset, and you get strong numbers on ImageNet, on segmentation, on retrieval. But all of those benchmarks were built by the same community, with the same priors about what a "task" is. They were, in many cases, scraped from the same internet. So when a model does well across them, you're partly measuring that your test distribution looks like your training distribution. That's not nothing, but it isn't evidence of generalizing to "every task."

The thing I find more revealing is where these models fail, because the failures cluster. They tend to fail on things that are rare on the web, or that humans don't bother to photograph and caption. Precise geometry, counting, fine spatial relations, anything that requires understanding the physical structure of a scene rather than recognizing what's in it. Medical imaging, satellite imagery, industrial inspection. The web is a very biased sample of visual experience. It's biased toward what people find interesting enough to upload, and that's a narrow slice of what a visual system in the world has to deal with.

So my first heuristic is actually a simple one. I ask whether the task has a natural caption. If the information you care about is something a person would plausibly write down next to the image, then a web-scale dataset probably covers it reasonably well. If it's something that lives purely in pixels and no one would ever describe in text, then I'm skeptical, and scale alone won't fix it, because you're scaling up the wrong signal.

The second thing I'd say is that we've been conflating breadth of the dataset with breadth of the learning signal. Some of our own work showed that if you take a modern architecture and train it in a very standard way on a much smaller dataset, you get a lot of the benefit that we had been attributing to data. Some of what looks like "the data is broad enough" is really "the recipe is good." That matters because it tells you the dataset isn't the whole story, and so you can't assess breadth by looking at the data in isolation.

And then there's a more fundamental limitation. Generalizing to every task is not a property you can verify from the inside. You can only ever test on tasks you've thought of. The right posture, I think, is less about trying to certify breadth and more about building the evaluation to hunt for the gaps. Deliberately go after distributions that are underrepresented on the web, check whether performance degrades gracefully or falls off a cliff, and look at whether the representations are actually encoding structure or just memorizing co-occurrence statistics.

So the short version is, I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you a dataset is broad enough. It's broad enough for the tasks we've been measuring. Whether it's broad enough for the next task is an empirical question every time, and the history of the field is that the next task usually finds the hole.

r001.rationale: The response proposes probing underrepresented distributions and downstream performance, but does not propose training a classifier to identify which dataset an image came from.

r002.rationale: It describes internet data as biased and benchmark evaluation as circular, but does not state that images make seemingly diverse datasets readily distinguishable from one another.

r003.rationale: The response says breadth cannot be certified from the inside and every new task requires empirical evaluation. It does not question whether a global distribution of computer vision images is a well-defined dataset target.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very hard to say that a dataset is broad enough for every task. Internet-scale data can be very large, but size is not the same as diversity. You can have many images that cover very similar things, while some domains are barely represented.

So I would assess this through transfer: train on that data, then evaluate on a wide range of tasks and distributions that weren’t part of training. And I would look beyond the average performance to see where the model fails. Does it still work when the image looks different, or when the task requires information that wasn’t important for the training objective?

Even if the model does well on all the benchmarks we have, that doesn’t establish that it will generalize to every task. It tells us that the data and the training method support those particular kinds of generalization. I think the useful question is where the coverage is missing, and what additional data would actually help.

r001.rationale: The response proposes transfer evaluation across tasks and distributions, not training a classifier to identify which dataset an image came from.

r002.rationale: It says large datasets may lack diversity, but does not claim that their images make the datasets readily distinguishable from one another.

r003.rationale: It questions whether data can support generalization to every task, but does not question whether a global image distribution is a well-defined dataset target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very difficult to say that a dataset is broad enough for every task, because we don’t know what every future task will look like. Internet-scale data can be enormous, but it still reflects what people choose to photograph and upload. So scale doesn’t necessarily mean coverage.

What we can do is evaluate the model across a diverse set of downstream tasks and domains, especially ones that differ from the training distribution. Does it transfer to medical images, satellite images, or tasks that require spatial understanding rather than recognizing an object? If it performs well across those settings, that gives us evidence of generality, but it’s not a guarantee.

So I would frame this as an empirical question: where does transfer work, where does it fail, and what data is missing in those failures? That’s more useful than declaring that an internet-scale dataset is universal.

r001.rationale: The response suggests evaluating transfer across downstream tasks and domains, but does not propose training a classifier to identify which dataset an image came from.

r002.rationale: It says internet-scale data reflects what people choose to photograph and upload, but does not state that different datasets remain readily distinguishable by their images.

r003.rationale: It questions whether data can be broad enough for every future task, but does not question whether a global distribution of computer vision images is a well-defined dataset target.
